graphs__course-schedule-i-ii.title: Course Schedule I/II
graphs__course-schedule-i-ii.pattern: Kahn's BFS topological sort / cycle detection
graphs__course-schedule-i-ii.statement: `numCourses` courses with prerequisites `[a, b]` meaning `b` must be taken before `a`. **I:** can all courses be finished (no cycle)? **II:** return a valid order (or `[]` if impossible).

examples.explanation: 0 first, then 1 and 2, then 3; [0,2,1,3] is also valid.

approaches.name: Kahn's algorithm (BFS on indegrees)
approaches.idea: Build adjacency `b -> a` and an indegree array. Seed a queue with all indegree-0 nodes. Pop a node, append it to the order, decrement its neighbors' indegrees, and enqueue any that reach 0. If the produced order contains all `numCourses` nodes it is valid; otherwise the leftover nodes form a cycle and no order exists.

graphs__course-schedule-i-ii.insight: Kahn's: repeatedly remove indegree-0 nodes. If you can't remove all of them, the leftover forms a cycle -> impossible. For Course Schedule I, just check `idx == numCourses`.

graphs__alien-dictionary.title: Alien Dictionary
graphs__alien-dictionary.pattern: Build precedence graph from adjacent words, then Kahn's topological sort
graphs__alien-dictionary.statement: Given a list of `words` sorted lexicographically by the rules of an unknown alien language, derive a possible order of its letters as a string. Return `""` if no valid order exists (e.g. a longer word appears before its own prefix).

examples.explanation: Comparing adjacent words yields t<f, w<e, r<t, e<r -> wertf.
A longer word precedes its prefix, which is invalid.

constraints: words[i] consists of only lowercase English letters

approaches.name: Precedence graph + Kahn's topological sort
approaches.idea: Only the first differing character between two adjacent words gives an ordering edge x -> y. Add every distinct letter as a node, derive edges from each adjacent pair (returning `""` if a word is a prefix of the previous longer word), then topologically sort. If the sort consumes every letter the string is a valid order; otherwise a cycle exists and the language is inconsistent.
approaches.time: O(C) where C is total characters

graphs__alien-dictionary.insight: Ordering info comes ONLY from the first differing char of adjacent words; guard the prefix case (`abc` before `ab` is invalid), then Kahn's over <=26 letters.

graphs__parallel-courses-ii.title: Parallel Courses II
graphs__parallel-courses-ii.pattern: Bitmask DP over course sets (topo + at-most-k-per-semester constraint)
graphs__parallel-courses-ii.statement: `n` courses, prerequisite edges `[a, b]` (a before b), and you may take up to `k` courses per semester (a course is available only once all its prereqs are done). Return the minimum number of semesters to finish all courses.

approaches.name: Subset DP over completed-course bitmasks
approaches.idea: `n <= 15` means state = bitmask of completed courses. For a state, `avail` is the set of not-yet-taken courses whose prereq mask is fully contained in the state. If at most `k` are available take all in one semester; otherwise enumerate every non-empty subset of `avail` of size <= k and transition, taking a min number of semesters. Greedily taking the k most-unlocking courses is a classic wrong answer, so all size-<=k subsets must be tried.

graphs__parallel-courses-ii.insight: `n <= 15` screams bitmask; you must try all size-<=k subsets of the currently-available set. `for (sub = mask; sub>0; sub=(sub-1)&mask)` enumerates subsets.

graphs__sort-items-by-groups-respecting-.title: Sort Items by Groups Respecting Dependencies
graphs__sort-items-by-groups-respecting-.pattern: Two-level topological sort (groups, then items within groups)
graphs__sort-items-by-groups-respecting-.statement: `n` items, each in a group (`-1` means its own singleton group). Given item dependencies `beforeItems`, return an ordering of items so that (a) items in the same group are contiguous and (b) all dependencies are respected. Return `[]` if impossible.

examples.explanation: One valid ordering: groups contiguous and every dependency satisfied.

approaches.name: Topo sort at two levels (groups and items)
approaches.idea: Give each `-1` item a fresh unique group id so every item has a real group. Build an item graph (item->item deps) and a group graph (a cross-group dependency `b -> a` adds group edge `groupOf(b) -> groupOf(a)`). Topo-sort items and topo-sort groups independently; if either can't consume all nodes there is a cycle so return `[]`. Otherwise bucket the item order by group and emit buckets in group-topo order.

graphs__sort-items-by-groups-respecting-.insight: Same-group-contiguous + cross deps = topo-sort the GROUPS and topo-sort the ITEMS independently, then lay items down grouped in group-topo order. Convert `-1` groups to unique ids first.

graphs__sequence-reconstruction.title: Sequence Reconstruction
graphs__sequence-reconstruction.pattern: Unique topological order check via Kahn's (queue size must stay 1)
graphs__sequence-reconstruction.statement: Given a permutation `org` of `1..n` and a list of subsequences `seqs`, decide whether `org` is the one and only shortest supersequence of all sequences in `seqs`. Equivalently, whether the precedence graph built from `seqs` has a unique topological order and that order is exactly `org`.

examples.explanation: Both [1,2,3] and [1,3,2] are valid supersequences, so reconstruction is not unique.
The order is forced to be exactly 1,2,3.

approaches.name: Kahn's with uniqueness enforcement
approaches.idea: Build a graph from consecutive elements of each subsequence and track distinct numbers. The reconstruction is unique iff at every step of Kahn's BFS the queue holds exactly one node, and that node matches `org` position by position. If the queue ever has more than one indegree-0 node the order is ambiguous; if the popped node diverges from `org`, or not all `n` numbers are covered, it fails.

graphs__sequence-reconstruction.insight: Unique topo order == the Kahn's queue never holds more than one node; also verify the distinct-number count equals n and each pop matches `org`.

graphs__redundant-connection-i-ii.title: Redundant Connection I/II
graphs__redundant-connection-i-ii.pattern: Union-Find to detect the cycle-closing edge (directed variant handles two-parent + cycle)
graphs__redundant-connection-i-ii.statement: A tree of `n` nodes had exactly one extra edge added. **I (undirected):** return the edge that can be removed so the result is a tree; if several, return the one appearing last. **II (directed):** the graph was a rooted tree plus one extra directed edge; return the edge to remove to restore a rooted tree (the last such edge in input).

examples.explanation: Edge [2,3] closes the cycle 1-2-3.
Node 3 gets two parents; removing [2,3] leaves a valid rooted tree.

approaches.name: I - Union-Find, first edge that fails to union
approaches.idea: Process edges in order and union their endpoints. The first edge whose two endpoints are already connected is the one that closes a cycle; since we scan in order this is automatically the last redundant edge for a single-extra-edge tree.

approaches.name: II - two-parent candidate + Union-Find cycle test
approaches.idea: The extra directed edge causes either a node with two parents, a cycle, or both. First detect a node with two incoming edges and record the two candidate edges (cand1 earlier, cand2 later). Then run Union-Find skipping cand2 if it exists: if a cycle appears with no two-parent case, that edge is the answer; if a cycle appears with a two-parent case, cand1 is the answer; if no cycle appears, cand2 is the answer.

graphs__redundant-connection-i-ii.insight: Undirected = first union failure. Directed = classify into two-parent vs cycle: record both candidate edges, retry Union-Find skipping the later one, and pick cand1/cand2/current edge from the outcome.

graphs__accounts-merge.title: Accounts Merge
graphs__accounts-merge.pattern: Union-Find over emails (shared email => same person)
graphs__accounts-merge.statement: Each account is `[name, email1, email2, ...]`. Two accounts belong to the same person if they share at least one email (names alone are not enough since people can share a name). Merge accounts, returning each merged account as the name followed by its emails in sorted order.

examples.explanation: The two Johns share b@x so they merge; Mary is separate.

constraints: emails are lowercase, name is alphabetic

approaches.name: Union-Find over email ids
approaches.idea: Assign each distinct email an integer id and remember its owner name. Within each account, union its first email with every other email so all of that account's emails join one component. Group emails by their DSU root, sort each group (a TreeSet keeps them sorted), and prepend the owner name.
approaches.time: O(N K log(N K)) for sorting, N accounts of up to K emails

graphs__accounts-merge.insight: Emails are the nodes, not accounts: map each email to an id, union all emails inside an account, then group by root and sort. The name is any email's owner.

graphs__number-of-islands-ii.title: Number of Islands II
graphs__number-of-islands-ii.pattern: Incremental Union-Find on a grid, maintaining a component count
graphs__number-of-islands-ii.statement: An `m x n` grid starts all water. Given `positions` where each turns a cell to land one at a time, return, after each addition, the number of islands (4-directionally connected land groups).

approaches.name: Union-Find with running island count
approaches.idea: Flatten each cell to `r*n + c`. When land is added, increment the count by one, then for each already-land neighbor attempt a union; every successful union merges two distinct islands so decrement the count. Skip positions that are already land (duplicates) to avoid double counting. Record the count after each step.

graphs__number-of-islands-ii.insight: Each new land cell first adds 1 island; every successful union with an existing-land neighbor subtracts 1. Guard duplicate positions.

graphs__most-stones-removed.title: Most Stones Removed
graphs__most-stones-removed.pattern: Union-Find on rows and columns; answer = stones - components
graphs__most-stones-removed.statement: Stones sit on a 2D plane, one per cell. A stone can be removed if another stone shares its row or column. Return the maximum number of stones that can be removed.

examples.explanation: All stones form one connected component, so all but one can be removed.

constraints: no two stones share the same coordinate

approaches.name: Union rows with columns, count components
approaches.idea: Within any connected component (stones linked through shared rows/columns) you can remove every stone except one, so the answer is `stones - components`. Model each row and each column as a node (offset columns to keep ids disjoint) and union a stone's row with its column. The number of distinct roots among used row/column nodes is the component count.

graphs__most-stones-removed.insight: Removable = total - number of connected components. Union each stone's row-node with its column-node (offset columns), then count distinct roots of used nodes.

graphs__smallest-string-with-swaps.title: Smallest String With Swaps
graphs__smallest-string-with-swaps.pattern: Union-Find components + sort characters within each component
graphs__smallest-string-with-swaps.statement: Given a string `s` and pairs of indices `pairs`, you may swap the characters at any given pair any number of times. Return the lexicographically smallest string obtainable.

examples.explanation: Swap (0,3) and (1,2) independently to sort each pair.
Indices 0,1,2,3 form one component, so it can be fully sorted.

constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters

approaches.name: Union-Find over indices, sort each component
approaches.idea: Swaps are transitive, so indices connected through pairs form a component whose characters can be freely rearranged. Union all paired indices, gather the indices of each component (in ascending order), sort that component's characters, and write the smallest characters back into the ascending index slots.

graphs__smallest-string-with-swaps.insight: Swappable indices form Union-Find components; within each component sort the chars and drop them into the component's ascending index positions.

graphs__number-of-good-paths.title: Number of Good Paths
graphs__number-of-good-paths.pattern: Process nodes by increasing value, Union-Find, count equal-max endpoints
graphs__number-of-good-paths.statement: Given a tree with node values `vals` and `edges`, count good paths. A good path has both endpoints with the same value and every node on the path has a value less than or equal to that endpoint value. Single-node paths count. Paths are undirected and counted once.

examples.explanation: 5 single-node paths plus the 3-3 path between nodes 1 and 4.

approaches.name: Union nodes in increasing value order
approaches.idea: Process values from smallest to largest. When handling value `v`, union each node of value `v` with any neighbor whose value is `<= v`; this guarantees every node currently in a component has value `<= v`, so `v` is the component's max. Group the value-`v` nodes by root: a root holding `c` such nodes contributes `c*(c-1)/2` good paths (every pair). Start the count at `n` for the single-node paths.

graphs__number-of-good-paths.insight: Add nodes by ascending value so each component's max is the current value; equal-max endpoints in the same component form good paths (`c` nodes -> C(c,2) pairs), plus n single-node paths.

graphs__making-a-large-island.title: Making a Large Island
graphs__making-a-large-island.pattern: Union-Find with component sizes; try flipping each 0 and sum distinct neighbor islands
graphs__making-a-large-island.statement: Given an `n x n` binary grid, you may change at most one `0` to `1`. Return the size of the largest island (4-directionally connected 1s) achievable afterward.

examples.explanation: Flip one 0 to join the two size-1 islands into size 3.
Already one island of size 4; no flip helps.

approaches.name: Union-Find islands, then evaluate each zero
approaches.idea: Union all adjacent 1s so every island has a root with a size. The base answer is the largest existing island. For each `0`, gather the DISTINCT island roots among its four neighbors (a set avoids double-counting the same island touched twice) and sum their sizes plus one for the flipped cell. Take the maximum over all zeros.

graphs__making-a-large-island.insight: Label islands with sizes via Union-Find, then for each 0 sum the sizes of the DISTINCT neighboring islands (+1); the set of roots prevents counting the same island twice.

graphs__network-delay-time.title: Network Delay Time
graphs__network-delay-time.statement: You are given a directed weighted graph of `n` nodes as `times[i] = [u, v, w]` (signal travels from `u` to `v` in `w` time). A signal starts at node `k`. Return the minimum time for all `n` nodes to receive it, or `-1` if some node is unreachable.

examples.explanation: Node 4 receives the signal last at time 2.

approaches.name: Dijkstra with min-heap
approaches.idea: The answer is the maximum over all nodes of the shortest-path distance from `k`. Run Dijkstra from `k`: pop the closest unsettled node, relax its edges. If any node stays at infinity it is unreachable, so return `-1`; otherwise return the largest finalized distance.

graphs__network-delay-time.insight: It is just Dijkstra: the network delay is the max of all shortest distances from the source.

graphs__cheapest-flights-within-k-stops.title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
graphs__cheapest-flights-within-k-stops.statement: Given `n` cities and `flights[i] = [from, to, price]`, find the cheapest price from `src` to `dst` using at most `k` stops (i.e. at most `k+1` edges). Return `-1` if there is no such route.

examples.explanation: 0->1->3 costs 700 using 1 stop; the cheaper 0->1->2->3 uses 2 stops and is not allowed.

approaches.name: Bellman-Ford, k+1 rounds
approaches.idea: Plain Dijkstra can prune a path that costs more but uses fewer stops, so it is wrong here. Instead do `k+1` Bellman-Ford relaxation rounds: each round relaxes every edge exactly once, so after round `i` we know the cheapest cost reachable with at most `i` edges. Relax from a frozen snapshot (`tmp = dist.clone()`) each round so one round cannot chain multiple hops.

graphs__cheapest-flights-within-k-stops.insight: When paths are constrained by number of edges, Bellman-Ford with a cloned snapshot per round beats Dijkstra.

graphs__path-with-minimum-effort.title: Path With Minimum Effort
graphs__path-with-minimum-effort.pattern: Dijkstra minimizing the maximum edge (minimax path)
graphs__path-with-minimum-effort.statement: Given a grid `heights`, travel from the top-left to the bottom-right moving 4-directionally. A route's effort is the maximum absolute height difference between consecutive cells on it. Return the minimum possible effort.

examples.explanation: The route 1->3->5->3->5 has max adjacent difference 2, better than going through 8.

approaches.name: Dijkstra on the minimax cost
approaches.idea: Define a cell's cost as the smallest possible value of the largest step needed to reach it. Run Dijkstra where relaxing an edge uses `max(currentEffort, |heightDiff|)` instead of a sum. Pop cells by increasing effort; the first time we pop the destination its effort is optimal.

graphs__path-with-minimum-effort.insight: Minimax path = Dijkstra where you relax with max() instead of sum().

graphs__swim-in-rising-water.title: Swim in Rising Water
graphs__swim-in-rising-water.pattern: Dijkstra minimizing the maximum cell value
graphs__swim-in-rising-water.statement: In an `n x n` grid, `grid[i][j]` is the elevation of that cell. At time `t` you can be on any cell whose elevation is at most `t`, and you can swim 4-directionally instantly between such cells. Return the least time to reach the bottom-right from the top-left.

examples.explanation: You must wait until time 3 so the cell with elevation 3 (bottom-right) is submerged and reachable.

approaches.name: Dijkstra on max elevation
approaches.idea: The time to reach a cell equals the minimum over all paths of the maximum elevation on that path. Run Dijkstra keyed by `max(pathMax, nextCellElevation)`; settle cells in increasing order of that key. The first time the bottom-right is popped gives the answer.

graphs__swim-in-rising-water.insight: Same minimax-Dijkstra trick as Path With Minimum Effort, but the cost is the cell value, not the edge difference.

graphs__minimum-cost-to-make-at-least-on.title: Minimum Cost to Make at Least One Valid Path
graphs__minimum-cost-to-make-at-least-on.statement: Each cell of an `m x n` grid holds a sign: `1` = right, `2` = left, `3` = down, `4` = up. Following the sign costs `0`; changing a cell's sign costs `1` and lets you leave in any direction. Starting at the top-left, return the minimum cost so at least one valid path reaches the bottom-right.

examples.explanation: Follow signs across each row and pay 1 to turn down at the end of rows 1, 2, and 3.

approaches.name: 0-1 BFS with a deque
approaches.idea: Model each cell as a node with 4 outgoing edges of weight 0 (the direction matching the sign) or 1 (the other three). With only 0/1 weights, 0-1 BFS runs Dijkstra in linear time: push zero-cost moves to the front of the deque and unit-cost moves to the back, so the deque stays monotonic in distance. `dist[m-1][n-1]` is the answer.

graphs__minimum-cost-to-make-at-least-on.insight: 0/1 edge weights => 0-1 BFS: front-push free moves, back-push paid ones, no heap needed.

graphs__reachable-nodes.title: Reachable Nodes
graphs__reachable-nodes.statement: Starting from an undirected graph of `n` nodes, each edge `[u, v, cnt]` is subdivided by inserting `cnt` new intermediate nodes. Starting at node `0` and moving at most `maxMoves` edges in the subdivided graph, return how many nodes (original + intermediate) are reachable.

examples.explanation: All 3 original nodes plus 10 subdivided nodes are reachable within 6 moves.

approaches.name: Dijkstra on original nodes, then account for edges
approaches.idea: An original edge with `cnt` intermediates has weight `cnt+1` in the compressed graph. Run Dijkstra from node `0` to get `dist[]` to every original node. Count reachable original nodes (`dist <= maxMoves`). For each edge, from `u` you can cover `max(0, maxMoves - dist[u])` intermediates and from `v` another `max(0, maxMoves - dist[v])`; the reachable intermediates on that edge are `min(cnt, u-side + v-side)`.

graphs__reachable-nodes.insight: Compress each subdivided edge to weight cnt+1, run Dijkstra on originals, then add min(cnt, budget from both ends) per edge.

graphs__shortest-path-in-a-grid-with-obs.title: Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination
graphs__shortest-path-in-a-grid-with-obs.pattern: BFS over 3D state (row, col, obstacles left)
graphs__shortest-path-in-a-grid-with-obs.statement: Given an `m x n` grid of `0` (empty) and `1` (obstacle), move 4-directionally from the top-left to the bottom-right. You may eliminate at most `k` obstacles. Return the fewest steps, or `-1` if impossible.

examples.explanation: Eliminating one obstacle lets a length-6 path reach the corner.

approaches.name: BFS on (cell, remaining eliminations)
approaches.idea: Unit-cost moves mean plain BFS gives shortest steps, but we must track remaining eliminations as part of the state, since reaching a cell with more budget left is strictly better. Visit `(r, c, remaining)`; step to a neighbor spending budget if it is an obstacle. A quick prune: if `k >= m+n-2` the Manhattan-distance path is always achievable.

graphs__shortest-path-in-a-grid-with-obs.insight: Add remaining eliminations to the BFS state so equal cells with different budgets are treated as distinct.

graphs__path-with-maximum-probability.title: Path with Maximum Probability
graphs__path-with-maximum-probability.pattern: Dijkstra with a max-heap on multiplicative weights
graphs__path-with-maximum-probability.statement: Given an undirected graph of `n` nodes with `edges[i] = [a, b]` and `succProb[i]` the success probability of that edge, return the maximum product of edge probabilities along any path from `start` to `end`. Return `0` if none exists.

examples.explanation: Path 0->1->2 has probability 0.5*0.5 = 0.25, better than the direct 0.2.

constraints: there is at most one edge between any two nodes

approaches.name: Dijkstra maximizing product
approaches.idea: Probabilities in [0,1] only shrink as a path grows, so the greedy Dijkstra invariant holds if we always expand the node with the largest current probability. Use a max-heap keyed by probability and relax with multiplication; the first time we pop `end` its probability is maximal.

graphs__path-with-maximum-probability.insight: Maximizing a product of values in [0,1] is Dijkstra with a max-heap and multiply-relax.

graphs__min-cost-to-connect-all-points.title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
graphs__min-cost-to-connect-all-points.statement: Given `points` on a 2D plane, the cost to connect two points is their Manhattan distance. Return the minimum total cost to connect all points so that any two are reachable (a minimum spanning tree).

examples.explanation: An MST over the Manhattan-distance complete graph has total cost 20.

approaches.name: Prim's algorithm (O(n^2) dense)
approaches.idea: The graph is complete (every pair is an edge), so a dense O(n^2) Prim beats heap-based Kruskal. Keep `minDist[v]` = cheapest edge connecting `v` to the growing tree. Each step pick the unused node with smallest `minDist`, add it, and relax all remaining nodes against it.

graphs__min-cost-to-connect-all-points.insight: Complete graph => dense O(n^2) Prim; no need to materialize all n^2 edges for a heap.

graphs__connecting-cities-with-minimum-c.title: Connecting Cities With Minimum Cost
graphs__connecting-cities-with-minimum-c.statement: There are `n` cities numbered `1..n`. `connections[i] = [c1, c2, cost]` is a bidirectional edge. Return the minimum total cost to connect all cities, or `-1` if impossible.

examples.explanation: Pick edges of cost 1 and 5 to connect all three cities.

approaches.name: Kruskal + union-find
approaches.idea: Sort edges by cost and greedily union endpoints that are in different components, accumulating cost. Path-compressed union-find makes each merge near O(1). A spanning tree needs exactly `n-1` accepted edges; if fewer are accepted the graph is disconnected, so return `-1`.

graphs__connecting-cities-with-minimum-c.insight: Kruskal: sort edges, union across components, and check you accepted exactly n-1 edges.

graphs__optimize-water-distribution.title: Optimize Water Distribution
graphs__optimize-water-distribution.pattern: MST with a virtual source node
graphs__optimize-water-distribution.statement: In a village of `n` houses you can either build a well in house `i` at cost `wells[i]`, or lay a pipe `pipes[j] = [h1, h2, cost]` to share water. Return the minimum total cost to supply water to every house.

examples.explanation: Build a well in house 1 (cost 1) and lay pipes 1-2 and 2-3 (cost 1 each).

approaches.name: Kruskal with virtual node 0
approaches.idea: Model 'building a well in house i' as a pipe of cost `wells[i]` from a virtual node `0` (an infinite water source) to house `i`. Then the whole problem is a single MST over `n+1` nodes: connecting a house to node `0` means it gets its own well, connecting to another house means shared piping. Run Kruskal over the combined edge list.

graphs__optimize-water-distribution.insight: Turn 'build a well' into an edge from a virtual super-source, then it is a plain MST.

graphs__find-critical-and-pseudo-critica.title: Find Critical and Pseudo-Critical Edges in MST
graphs__find-critical-and-pseudo-critica.statement: Given a weighted undirected graph, an edge is critical if deleting it increases the MST weight, and pseudo-critical if it can appear in some MST but is not critical. Return the two lists of original edge indices.

examples.explanation: Edges 0 and 1 are in every MST (critical); edges 2,3,4,5 appear in some MST (pseudo-critical).

approaches.name: Compare MST weight with each edge forced/excluded
approaches.idea: Compute the base MST weight. For each edge: build an MST that excludes it; if the resulting weight is larger (or the graph disconnects), the edge is critical. Otherwise force the edge into the MST first and build; if that still equals the base weight, the edge is pseudo-critical. Keep original indices while sorting a copy by weight.

graphs__find-critical-and-pseudo-critica.insight: Critical => excluding it raises MST weight; pseudo-critical => forcing it in still ties the MST weight.

graphs__critical-connections-in-a-networ.title: Critical Connections in a Network
graphs__critical-connections-in-a-networ.statement: A network of `n` servers is connected by undirected `connections`. A connection is critical if removing it disconnects some servers. Return all critical connections (bridges) in any order.

examples.explanation: Edge 1-3 is the only bridge; the triangle 0-1-2 has no bridge.

approaches.name: Tarjan's bridge algorithm
approaches.idea: Do a DFS assigning each node a discovery time `disc[u]` and a low-link `low[u]` = the earliest discovery time reachable from `u`'s subtree via at most one back edge. Edge `(u, v)` (v a child) is a bridge exactly when `low[v] > disc[u]`, meaning `v`'s subtree has no alternative route back to `u` or above.

graphs__critical-connections-in-a-networ.insight: Bridge test: DFS with low-links, edge (u,v) is a bridge iff low[v] > disc[u].

graphs__reconstruct-itinerary.title: Reconstruct Itinerary
graphs__reconstruct-itinerary.statement: Given a list of airline `tickets [from, to]`, reconstruct the itinerary that uses all tickets exactly once, starting at `JFK`. If multiple valid itineraries exist, return the lexicographically smallest one.

examples.explanation: The unique Eulerian path using every ticket once.

approaches.name: Hierholzer with lexical min-heaps
approaches.idea: This is an Eulerian path (use every edge once). Store each airport's destinations in a min-heap so we always try the smallest next airport. Run Hierholzer: push the current node, if it has an unused outgoing edge follow the smallest; otherwise it is a dead end, pop it to the front of the route. Reversing the post-order dead-ends yields the lexicographically smallest valid path.

graphs__reconstruct-itinerary.insight: Eulerian path via Hierholzer: greedily follow smallest edges, prepend dead-ends, no backtracking needed.

graphs__valid-arrangement-of-pairs.title: Valid Arrangement of Pairs
graphs__valid-arrangement-of-pairs.statement: Given `pairs[i] = [start_i, end_i]`, arrange all pairs into a sequence so that for every adjacent pair, `end` of the current equals `start` of the next. A valid arrangement is guaranteed to exist; return any one.

examples.explanation: Each pair's end matches the next pair's start, forming one chain.

approaches.name: Hierholzer on the directed graph
approaches.idea: Treat each pair `[u, v]` as a directed edge `u -> v`; a valid arrangement is an Eulerian path. The start node is the unique vertex with `outdegree - indegree == 1` if it exists, otherwise any vertex with edges (Eulerian circuit). Run iterative Hierholzer to get the node visiting order, then emit consecutive nodes as the pairs.

graphs__valid-arrangement-of-pairs.insight: Pairs form directed edges; an Eulerian path from the out-in==1 vertex gives the arrangement.

graphs__minimize-malware-spread.title: Minimize Malware Spread
graphs__minimize-malware-spread.statement: Given an undirected graph as adjacency matrix `graph` and a list `initial` of initially infected nodes, malware spreads to every node in an infected node's connected component. Remove exactly one node from `initial` to minimize the final number of infected nodes. Return the node to remove (smallest index on ties).

examples.explanation: Nodes 0 and 1 share a component with two infected sources, so removing either saves nobody there; return the smaller index 0.

approaches.name: Union-find, remove the sole infector of the largest component
approaches.idea: Union all connected nodes, then compute each component's size and how many initial infected nodes it contains. Removing a node helps only if it is the *only* infected node in its component, since otherwise the component still gets infected by another source. Among such nodes pick the one whose component is largest (ties broken by smallest index). If none qualifies, return the smallest index in `initial`.

graphs__minimize-malware-spread.insight: Removing a source only helps if it is the unique infected node in its component; then favor the largest such component.
